pirates_n_ships.almanac.not_yet.p1.text1: An honest chart leaves blank what nobody has sailed. These are the waters this Almanac cannot yet describe, because nobody has built them yet.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.not_yet.p2.list1: **Oars** to move a big ship in a flat calm.
**A ship's logbook** to record your voyages and deeds.
**Paint for the hull,** to dye her planks your own colours.
**A wanted poster** of your own, beyond the chat, the notice board and the rank box.
**Feints of your own** with the sword, and a way to choose the side of your cut and your parry.
**Sounds of their own** for most of the work aboard: until then, the creak of the hull, the shanties and the guns must do.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.not_yet.p2.text1: If you find something in these pages that the sea does not do, or something the sea does that these pages do not tell, the mistake is the Almanac's. Tell whoever keeps your server.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.not_yet.title: Not yet charted
pirates_n_ships.almanac.provisions.p1.te: An empty pantry sinks more ships than cannon ever did. Every dawn your crew eats and drinks one day's provisions from the stores aboard. Keep the stores full and the crew stays willing; let them run dry and you will soon be sailing alone.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.provisions.p2.li: Anything edible counts, by how filling it is. One hand needs about a loaf of bread and a bit each day.
The crew eats what will spoil first, and turns up its nose at rotten flesh, spider eyes and other foul fare.
Sneak and use it with both hands empty to read what it holds and what spoils next.
A hopper can only put provisions in, and only takes out what is no provision: empty bottles, bowls, rotten flesh. A hopper below makes a fine waste chute.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.provisions.p2.te: The {item:pirates_n_ships:pantry}**pantry** (eight planks around a sheaf of wheat) is the ship's food store: 27 slots that open like a chest. Its doors face you when you place it.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.provisions.p3.li: {item:pirates_n_ships:hardtack}**Hardtack:** three wheat and a water bucket make two.
{item:pirates_n_ships:salted_fish}**Salted fish:** a cod or salmon and dried kelp.
{item:pirates_n_ships:salt_pork}**Salt pork:** a porkchop and dried kelp.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.provisions.p3.te: Fresh food spoils after five days in the pantry and turns to rotten flesh.
Preserved food never spoils: bread, cookies, dried kelp, honey bottles, golden carrots and golden apples, and the sailor's own:
pirates_n_ships.almanac.provisions.p4.li: A water bucket pours in 3 rations, a bottle 1. An empty bucket draws 3 out, a glass bottle 1.
Rain slowly fills a barrel that stands under the open sky.
The top shows how full it is, and a broken barrel keeps its water.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.provisions.p4.te: A {item:pirates_n_ships:water_barrel}**water barrel** holds 16 rations of fresh water, and each hand drinks one a day. It is crafted full from planks, iron nuggets and a water bucket.
Water and rum count wherever they are stowed, in a pantry or a barrel.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.provisions.p5.te: A crew short of food loses heart by the day and works at three quarters of its pace. A crew short of water loses heart far faster and works at half. Both together are a ship of the half-dead. Low spirits end in desertion; see [[pirates_n_ships:crew|Crew]]. Three days in a row without food, or a single day without water, and the whole crew deserts at the next dawn, however cheerful.
After eight days without fresh food, scurvy sets in: the crew weakens and loses heart every day. Any fresh food cures it, and fruit best of all: apples, melon, berries.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.provisions.p6.te: {item:pirates_n_ships:rum}**Rum** is made from sugar cane, two sugar and a glass bottle. While there is rum aboard, every hand gets a ration a day and his spirits rise for it. Stow rum for ten days or more in the pantries and the crew drinks a double ration: drunk, it works at little more than half its pace until the binge is over.
You may drink it yourself: it warms you through for two minutes and leaves the bottle.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.provisions.p7.te: Swimming or wading in frozen or cold seas and frozen rivers chills you like powder snow: after some seven seconds you are frozen and take hurt.
You are safe in a boat, on deck or in a dry hold, in any piece of leather armour, or with a bottle of rum in you. Swimming anywhere makes you hungry half again as fast as it otherwise would.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.provisions.p8.te: Prisoners in your brig eat and drink too, half a hand's share, and get no rum. See [[pirates_n_ships:law|Law]].
pirates_n_ships.almanac.provisions.title: Provisions
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p1.text1: A ship is only as good as the hand who sails her. Learn the wind, learn your canvas, and learn to keep the bow where you want it. The rest is patience.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p10.head: The gangway
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p10.text: The {item:pirates_n_ships:boarding_plank}**boarding plank** is your gangway in port as much as in a fight. Use it on the edge of your deck or rail toward the quay, or on the quay's edge toward your ship: it bridges up to six blocks and climbs or falls up to two on stepped ramps, so a deck that rides low under a high pier is no trouble. Laid from the pier or from the ship, it lies on the ship and goes where she goes; between two piers it is plain planking. A moored ship may heave in a storm without snapping it, but let her drift a block and a half along the quay and it breaks. Sneak and use it with an empty hand, from either end, to stow it.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p11.head: Waves and weather
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p11.text: The sea follows the weather. In fair weather there is a low swell or a light chop; in rain the sea runs rough; in a thunderstorm the crests stand two blocks and more above the still water. The change comes over about a minute.
Waves come in sets: a run of bigger seas, then a calmer spell. Your ship rises on the crests and sinks in the troughs, a small boat far more than a big one, and in heavy weather the bow throws spray.

A rowing boat rides the swell too, climbing the same crests out on open water, and anything you throw overboard bobs along with it; on lakes, rivers and in the shallows by the shore the water lies still as ever.
In rough seas every open hatch or low rim near the waterline takes water at the crests. Close your hatches and keep a pump manned before a storm.
A moving ship leaves a wake: a bow wave spreading from the stem and a trail of foam astern that fades over some seconds.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p12.head: Ratlines
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p12.list: Click the side of a mast to hang a net on it like a ladder.
Click the top of the deck or the gunwale to lay a sloped net instead. It rises at 45° the way you face, so stand at the gunwale looking at the mast.
Click a ratline you placed to add the next one at the end of its run, straight up a hanging net or up and forward along a sloped one.
Sneak to place against the clicked side instead.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p12.text: {item:pirates_n_ships:ratlines}**Ratlines** are rope nets for climbing aloft, to a crow's nest or a yard.

Climb a hanging net like a ladder; walk up a sloped one. A net needs something to rest on: break one and the nets that hung from it fall too. A sloped run may end on a yard right beside the mast, and from there you climb straight on up the hanging net above.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p13.head: Ratline nets
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p13.text: {item:pirates_n_ships:ratline_net}A **ratline net** runs from a **chainplate** at the rail to a **mast hoop** up the mast, at any slope from 30° to straight up. Put the chainplate on top of the rail or on its side and the hoop on the mast, then use the net on one and then on the other. The line between their rings must be clear of blocks and at most 32 blocks long; you are told what is wrong otherwise. Walk into the net and hold forward or jump to climb it along its line; sneak to hold on. Up to five nets from different chainplates can share one hoop: string three chainplates along the rail to the same hoop and the space between them is netted too, a triangle wide at the rail and pointed at the hoop that you can climb anywhere (chainplates more than 6 blocks apart stay separate nets). Break a net, its chainplate or put a block into it and that net comes down and drops at its chainplate; the rest of the triangle closes up again, and breaking the hoop drops them all. The net sails with the ship.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p14.head: The ship's bell
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p14.text: The {item:pirates_n_ships:ships_bell}**ship's bell** sits on a post or a wall. Right-click it and it swings and rings.
It is a bell and nothing more: it does not call your crew. But mark it when you lie in a harbour: when raiders come, every bell in the settlement rings the alarm.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p15.head: The crow's nest
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p15.list: **Ships**, by the flag they fly: a merchant, a navy ship, a pirate ship, a wreck, or just a sail.
**Land**, the nearest coast, once per stretch of shore.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p15.text: The {item:pirates_n_ships:crows_nest}**crow's nest** is a barrel for the masthead. Place it on a log, a fence, a wall or any block with a solid top; if that block goes, the nest falls. Climb up the mast and step in over the rim, and sneak to stay put.
Whoever stands in the nest keeps the lookout, you or a hand you post there with the whistle. Every few seconds the lookout sweeps 160 blocks around the ship and calls what is new to everyone aboard:

A call is short. One line appears over your hotbar, "Sail two points to starboard, 140 blocks" or "Land ahead, 300 blocks", a small bell rings up in the nest, and a diamond lights on the rim of your compass where the sighting lies: white for land, red for a pirate, blue for the navy, grey for the rest. The mark fades after half a minute. Nothing goes to chat.

Bearings are called from the bow: ahead, so many points to starboard or port (a full circle is 32 points), abeam, on the quarter, astern. The lookout calls each sighting once, then again when it has closed in a good way or after two minutes, and remembers it a while after it drops from view.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p16.head: The ship's panels
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p16.list: **The compass,** bottom left: a ship-shaped needle points along your heading, the wind arrow sits outside the rose, and below it you read the speed in knots and the rudder angle.
**The hull strip,** bottom right: one cell per compartment from bow to stern, filling blue as water comes in, with a red mark at a breach and a pump sign where a pump works.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p16.text: While you are aboard, two small panels watch over her.

They stay while you walk the deck, climb the rigging or stand at the helm, and go a moment after you leave her. Her name, load and crew are on the ship screen at the helm; see [[pirates_n_ships:ships|Ships]].
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p17.head: Music at sea
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p17.text: Aboard, the next tune is a sea shanty; at sea but not aboard, an air of wind and water. A tune is never cut off, and a few minutes of quiet pass between them.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p2.text1: Every sea has one wind, the same for every soul on it. It blows from one quarter at a time, between a light air and a fresh gale, and it veers and freshens slowly through the day.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p2.text2: Rain stiffens it by half again, and a thunderstorm more than doubles it and brings sudden gusts.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p2.text3: You can read the wind without instruments. Out on the water, thin white streaks drift past from where it comes, more of them and faster the harder it blows. Flags stream downwind, and set sails belly out to leeward.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p2.text4: Aboard, the compass rose at the bottom of your view carries a pale arrow on the side the wind comes from. The longer the arrow, the stronger the wind; it glows amber in a gust.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p3.show_: Show me: rigging a sail and working the winch
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p3.text1: A square sail hangs between two {item:pirates_n_ships:yard}**yards**. A yard is a row of yard blocks laid end to end across the mast; its middle block marks the mast.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p3.text2: **1.** Set the upper yard across the mast.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p3.text3: **2.** Set a second yard of the same direction 2 to 8 blocks straight below it. Between the two middle blocks there may be only air or mast (logs, fences).
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p3.text4: **3.** The pair is now one sail. The cloth is drawn between them; you place no canvas blocks.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p3.text5: The sail's area is the yards' mean length times the drop between them: two yards 5 wide and 5 apart give 25. A yard may be up to 15 blocks long. Three yards on one mast make two sails.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p3.text6: A square sail loves a wind from astern and is useless within 45° of the wind.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p3.text7: Click a yard that heads no sail and it tells you what is wrong with the rig.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p4.text1: A triangular sail is rigged with {item:pirates_n_ships:rope}**rope** and three {item:pirates_n_ships:cleat}**cleats**.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p4.text2: **1.** Put one cleat high on the side of the mast: the head.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p4.text3: **2.** Put one on the deck or a bowsprit further forward, at least 2 blocks lower: the tack.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p4.text4: **3.** Put one straight below the head: the clew.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p4.text5: **4.** Use a rope on the head cleat, then on the tack cleat, no more than 16 blocks away. The rope is spent and a stay runs between them.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p4.text6: The cloth fills the triangle between the stay and the clew. Its area is half of head-to-tack times head-to-clew. A fore-and-aft sail is the one for a wind on the beam: it still drives at 45° off the wind.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p4.text7: Click the head cleat with an empty hand to work its trim. Break the clew and the cloth goes but the stay stays; break the tack and you get your rope back.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p4.text8: A rope between two cleats or mooring rings that is no stay becomes a rope line: a sagging rope for a rail or a rigging. Each cleat or ring holds up to four.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p5.list1: Use the {item:pirates_n_ships:sail_winch}**sail winch** on deck to work **every** sail of the ship together: furled, then half, then full, then furled again.
Click an upper yard, or the head cleat of a triangular sail, with an empty hand to work that one sail alone.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p5.text1: Every sail has three trims: furled, half and full. Half sail draws half the force of full.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p5.text2: The force grows with the wind you feel on board, the area of the canvas and its trim. No sail drives within 30° of the wind, and a ship running before the wind never outruns it. Sails work only on a ship afloat.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p5.text3: You need not brace the yards: the crew is assumed to trim every sail as well as it can be trimmed. Watch the cloth instead. A sail that draws bellies out to leeward; a sail that shakes and hangs slack is in the no-go zone, and you must bear away.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p5.text4: Your hull holds you on course. A ship slides ahead far more easily than sideways, so a beam wind drives her forward instead of pushing her to leeward. No keel block is needed.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p6.show_: Show me: steering at the helm
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p6.text1: Hold right-click on the {item:pirates_n_ships:helm}**helm** of an assembled ship to take the wheel. Then move the mouse, or hold A and D, to turn it: right or D puts her to starboard, left or A to port. The wheel turns three quarters of a turn each way from midships.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p6.text2: The line above your hotbar shows the rudder angle, up to 35° either side. Let go and the wheel stays where you left it.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p6.text3: The rudder bites only while the ship moves through the water, and it works the other way round when she makes sternway. A slow ship turns on the same circle as a fast one; she just takes longer to sail it.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p6.text4: If your server has turned off steering by dragging, click the wheel instead: its right third one step to starboard, its left third to port, the middle back to midships.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p7.text1: Wind on the side of a sail heels the ship over, and the hull rights itself. A wide, shallow hull stands stiffest. As the heel nears 25°, the sails spill their wind, so no storm will lay a sound ship on her side under canvas alone.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p7.text2: The shipwright ballasts every ship as you built her: a tall stern castle or a heavy gun deck on one side does not tip her. What you load later does. Cargo stowed to one side and water in the hold make her list; pump her dry and trim the load, as [[pirates_n_ships:trade|Cargo and trade]] explains.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p7.text3: A long, wide hull stands steadier than a short, narrow one. Build her with some beam if you mean to carry a press of sail.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p8.list1: Use the capstan to let go. The anchor sinks fast, with the chain rattling, and lands a few blocks astern if you still had way on.
Once it bites, the chain pulls her up gently at the bow. She swings round toward the capstan's side and lies head to her chain.
She counts as anchored once the anchor holds and she has stopped.
Use the capstan again to weigh: the chain comes in at a steady pace and drags the anchor up to the hull. Use it again midway to let go once more.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p8.show_: Show me: dropping and weighing anchor
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p8.text1: The {item:pirates_n_ships:capstan}**capstan** works the anchor. The anchor hangs outside the hull on the capstan's side, just below the deck.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p8.text2: The chain is 32 blocks long. Over deeper water the capstan refuses to let go, for the anchor would find no bottom.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p8.text3: A ship pulling harder than her anchor holds drags it over the seabed. Furl before you anchor.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p9.text1: There are no mooring lines to belay at a quay: a ship tied up is simply a ship lying still at the berth. Bring her in slowly, drop the anchor, and she is moored. A harbour counts your ship as moored at its port once she lies within about 32 blocks of it.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.p9.text2: {item:pirates_n_ships:mooring_ring}**Mooring rings** and **cleats** serve the grappling hook. A hook flying close to a ring catches on it, and a hook held by a ring holds twice as far before it tears loose. With your hook set in another ship, use a ring or a cleat on your own ship to make the rope fast there; the ships keep hauling together and you can walk away. A ring on land holds a hooked ship the same way. The [[pirates_n_ships:combat|Weapons and combat]] chapter tells the rest of the hook.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.sailing.title: Sailing
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p1.heading: Ships
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p1.text1: A ship is a heap of timber that has agreed to float. Treat her well, know what she can bear, and mend her quickly when she is hurt.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p10.list1_: A {item:pirates_n_ships:nameplate}**nameplate** (any sign and a gold nugget) shows her name once she is launched and named.

A **figurehead** for the bow: a mermaid, lion, eagle or skull, from four planks and a prismarine shard, gold ingot, feather or bone. Click the hull block it should hang on, and the figure looks toward you.
The {item:pirates_n_ships:ship_lantern}**ship's lantern** stands on deck, hangs from a beam or from a bracket on a wall, and burns even under water.
{item:pirates_n_ships:stern_window}**Stern windows** go into a wall from outside; right-click to open or close the shutters.
{item:pirates_n_ships:rope_coil}**Rope coils** stack four to a spot.
The {item:pirates_n_ships:chart_table}**chart table** is a captain's table with a chart spread on it.
The {item:pirates_n_ships:sea_cot}**sea cot** is a wooden bed for the great cabin. Sleep in it aboard and you lie in it as she sails, and wake and respawn at it wherever she has gone.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p10.text1: A ship should look the part.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p11.text1: The shipwrights of the seafarer villages build to order. Open the harbour master's desk and turn to the **Orders** tab: each ship shows her price in doubloons, the days he needs, and the logs and wool he wants. Any logs and any wool will do.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p11.text2: **1.** Carry the doubloons and the materials, and press **Order**. You receive a {item:pirates_n_ships:ship_receipt}**ship receipt**; its tooltip counts the days.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p11.text3: **2.** When it reads "Ready for pickup", use the same port's desk with the receipt in hand.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p11.text4: **3.** Your ship lies assembled at a free berth beside the pier, and she is yours.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p11.text5: A shipwright builds at most three ships at once. If both berths are taken, come back later: the receipt stays good. Armed sloops are never for sale; you earn one by rank or take one at sea (see [[pirates_n_ships:law|Law]] and [[pirates_n_ships:combat|Weapons and combat]]).
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p12.list1_: **Keep near the middle of the world.** Very far from the world's centre, many tens of thousands of blocks out, ships stop moving true.
**Water under the hull.** A ship floats only on the water beneath her own hull; a ship in a dry dock beside the sea stays put.
**Load trims her.** The shipwright ballasts her level as you built her, but cargo and flood water make her list and sit lower.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p2.heading: Launching at the helm
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p2.list1_1: Every block joined to the helm, face to face or edge to edge, becomes part of her.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p2.list1_2: Air, water and natural ground never join: dirt, sand, raw stone, ores, gravel, ice, snow, leaves, coral and kelp stay where they are. Logs and planks are no ground, so a wooden ship is whole.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p2.list1_3: A ship may hold up to 2048 blocks. A bigger one the helm refuses, and says so. A dock that touches the hull counts toward the limit, so keep a gap.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p2.list1_4: Chests and barrels keep what is in them.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p2.list1_5: The sea closes over the place where she was built; no hole is left in the water.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p2.show_me: Show me: building and assembling a ship
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p2.text1: Using a {item:pirates_n_ships:helm}**helm** that stands in the world launches a ship:
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p2.text2: Your ship gets a name and an owner: you. Use a **name tag** on her helm to rename her.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p3.heading: The ship screen
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p3.list1_1: **Ship:** her name (type a new one and press Rename), the flag she flies, her hull (compartments, flooding, breaches, pumps), her load and speed, the anchor, the sails, crew and bunks, the days of supplies left and the last payday. **Disassemble**, pressed twice, takes her apart.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p3.list1_2: **Crew:** buttons for every whistle order, then every hand aboard with his morale, station, order and pay. **Release** takes a hand off his station; **Dismiss** lets him go.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p3.list1_3: **Stations:** every station aboard, who works it and what he does. **Man** lists your free hands; pick one with **Send** and he goes there and stays.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p3.text1: Sneak and use the helm of your own ship with an empty hand to open the ship screen. It has three tabs.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p3.text2: Only the owner opens the screen; others are told she is not their ship. Step more than 8 blocks from the helm and it closes.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p4.heading: Taking her apart
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p4.list1_3: something solid is in the way (you are told where).
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p4.text1: Press **Disassemble** twice on the ship screen. She becomes blocks again, set square to the world with her heading turned to the nearest quarter. It is refused when:
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p4.text2: Players and beasts on deck are set down on the deck blocks, and any water inside the hull is let out.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p4.text3: If her helm is broken she stays a ship: her stations still work, but nothing steers or takes her apart until you place a new helm anywhere on her deck.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p5.heading: The dry hold
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p5.list1_1: **Watertight:** full blocks, slabs, stairs and glass.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p5.list1_2: **Not watertight:** fences, walls, bars, panes, ladders and chains.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p5.list1_3: **Doors, trapdoors and fence gates** are openings: watertight when shut, a way in for water when open.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p5.text1: A ship knows her own hull. Any room that lies below the lowest place water could pour in stays dry: a closed cabin is dry, and an open boat is dry up to her rim. Inside the dry part there is no water: you walk and breathe as on land.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p5.text2: The dry volume under the waterline is what keeps her up. Flood water weighs her down, and a ship flooded through is a ship on the bottom.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p6.heading: Flooding
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p6.list1_1: Rooms joined by an open door or hatch fill together. A shut door holds the water back.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p6.list1_2: Placing any block into the breach stops the flow.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p6.list1_3: Flood water shows as a level surface in the room, rising and falling with the flood.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p6.text1: A hull block destroyed below the waterline is a breach, and the sea pours into the room behind it. So does an open hatch or door below the waterline. The bigger and deeper the hole, the faster the water comes: a single hole one block under lets in about a block of water every second.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p6.text2: Below that surface you hold your breath as in the sea. Get your head clear of the water, or drown in your own hold.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p7.heading: Pumps
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p7.text1: Craft a {item:pirates_n_ships:bilge_pump}**bilge pump** from a stick, three planks and a bucket. Place it on the hold floor, or on the deck right above the hold: its pipe reaches 4 blocks down through the planks.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p7.text2: Hold right-click on it to pump. It lifts one block of water a second and stops when you let go. Your view tells you how much water is left, or that the bilge is dry. It drains the highest flooded room below it, and several pumps in one room add up.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p7.text3: Pumping is hard work and makes you hungry. Post a hand at the pump with the whistle and order **Man the pumps**: he pumps until the room is dry.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p8.heading: Patching a breach
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p8.show_me: Show me: patching and mending a hull
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p8.text1: A {item:pirates_n_ships:hull_patch}**hull patch** is a tarred plank; two planks and a lump of coal or charcoal make two. Stand inside, look at the edge of the hole (the face of a hull block beside it) and use the patch. It fills the hole and the water stops at once.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p8.text2: A patch goes only into a real hole in an assembled ship; anywhere else it tells you so and is not spent. You may break a patch later and put in a proper plank, but the hole is open while you swap.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p9.heading: When she breaks in two
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p9.text1: Shoot or break the only block joining two parts of a ship and she splits. The part with the helm stays your ship; the other becomes a wreck that drifts but no longer sails, and its nameplate reads "Wreck of" her name. Pieces of fewer than four blocks fall apart into items.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p9.text2: You can nail her together again with a {item:pirates_n_ships:shipwright_toolkit}**shipwright's toolkit**: a {item:pirates_n_ships:carpenters_hammer}**carpenter's hammer**, a {item:pirates_n_ships:saw}**saw**, {item:pirates_n_ships:nails}**nails** and leather. Three iron nuggets make eight nails.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p9.text3: **1.** Sneak and use the toolkit on the part you keep, usually the one with the helm. While you hold the toolkit, green sparkles show where the pieces meet.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p9.text4: **2.** Bring the broken piece back against her, lined up straight and touching face to face. Bridge a one-block gap with planks first.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p9.text5: **3.** Use the toolkit on the broken piece. After a moment of hammering it is nailed back on, with its chests and stations, and she keeps her name.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.p9.text6: Each repair takes 4 nails. Only pieces of the same ship join, and only pieces of up to 200 blocks.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.ships.title: Ships
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p1.heading: Cargo and trade
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p1.text1: Buy where a thing is cheap, carry it where it is wanted, and sell it dear. That is the whole of honest trade, and a fine living it makes for a captain with a sound hold and a steady nerve.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p10.text1: A navy outpost charges a small docking fee of 5 doubloons when your ship ties up at a berth or anchors inside it, once a day per ship. It comes from your purse, or from the coin in your ship's chests. Leave it unpaid and the outpost's desk will not trade with you until you settle it, coin in hand. Captains the navy trusts well, and officers from Lieutenant up, dock for free. Sailing through costs nothing.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p11.text1: A port offers delivery contracts: carry an amount of a good to another port by a deadline for a reward. Accepting costs a deposit of a fifth of the reward; delivering at the far port's desk pays the reward and gives the deposit back. You may hold three at a time.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p12.list1_: **Hunts:** pirates, sharks or, rarely, the kraken; or a pirate island's named captain.
**Cargo runs:** a contract with a raised reward and no deposit.
**Treasure hunts:** you get a treasure map; open the chest at the X.
**Escorts:** keep within 96 blocks of a merchant ship on at least half her course and see her into port.
**Raids and patrols:** pirate islands want convoys plundered or navy patrols sunk; navy outposts want pirate ships sunk or taken.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p12.text1: Every desk offers up to three quests, renewed every two days. Accept up to three at once; each must be done within five days.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p12.text2: A quest pays doubloons and raises your standing with whoever gave it.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p2.heading: Crates and barrels
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p2.list1_1: {item:pirates_n_ships:cargo_crate}**Cargo crate** (four planks and four sticks): 32 stacks of one item.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p2.list1_2: {item:pirates_n_ships:cargo_barrel}**Cargo barrel** (six planks and two iron nuggets): 1536 items of one kind, whatever their stack size; best for rum and other small stacks.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p2.text1: Bulk cargo goes in containers that hold **one kind of item** in great amounts.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p2.text2: Use one with a stack to put it in, with an empty hand to take a stack out, and sneak-use with an empty hand to put in everything of that kind you carry. Items that do not stack are refused, and stolen and clean goods of the same kind never share a container. A broken container keeps its cargo, and hoppers work on it.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p3.heading: Weight and trim
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p3.text1: Cargo weighs. Crates, cargo barrels, pantries and water barrels grow heavier as they fill: a full crate weighs as much as forty planks. A chest presses down where it stands, so a heavy chest in the bow trims her by the head.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p3.text2: Spread heavy cargo and keep it low and amidships. A laden ship sits deeper, floods sooner through a breach, and is slower to gather way and to turn.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p3.text3: The ship screen at the helm reads her load: Light, Laden, Heavily laden or Overloaded.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p4.heading: The sea chest
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p4.list1_1: Use it in the air to carry it on your back. You cannot jump, sprint or swim, you walk slower, and in water it drags you under.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p4.list1_2: Place it on water and it floats, drifting with wind and current.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p4.list1_3: Use it to open it, sneak-use to pick it up, or strike it to knock it loose as an item.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p4.text1: The {item:pirates_n_ships:sea_chest}**sea chest** (three leather over iron, a chest and iron) holds 54 stacks and keeps them when broken, carried or floated.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p4.text2: A {item:pirates_n_ships:paddle}**paddle** (two planks and a stick) turns a floating chest into a boat of sorts: use the paddle on it to sit on the lid, then paddle forward and back and turn left and right. Sneak to get off. You cannot open the chest while you sit on it.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p5.heading: Doubloons
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p5.list1_1: by selling goods at a harbour master's desk,
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p5.list1_2: from the purses of slain pirates and pirate captains,
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p5.list1_3: from the chests of wrecks and buried treasure,
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p5.list1_4: from bounties, ransoms, delivery contracts, quests and prize money.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p5.text1: The gold {item:pirates_n_ships:doubloon}**doubloon** is the coin of the sea. Nobody mints it; you earn it:
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p5.text2: Carry them in your inventory; that is where the markets take them from.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p6.heading: Harbours
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p6.list1_1: **Seafarer villages** stand on beaches: a stone quay with the harbour master's hut, a pier with two berths, cottages, a tavern and a shipwright's shed.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p6.list1_2: **Navy outposts** are stone forts on beaches, rarer than villages: a sea gate, a quay with two berths, cannon on the walls and a garrison that never leaves its posts. An officer stands by the office door.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p6.list1_3: **Pirate islands** are camps on beaches, rarer still: a jetty, tents, a tavern, a captain's hut and a fence's shack under the Jolly Roger. Strangers are not welcome.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p6.text1: The coast has three kinds of port, each with a harbour master's desk.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p6.text2: A desk you place inside a port joins that port.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p7.heading: The harbour master
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p7.list1_1: **Goods:** every good the port trades, with your doubloons. Green goods are made here and cheap to buy; orange goods are wanted here and good to sell. Pick a quantity, then Buy or Sell; the prices shown are for the whole quantity.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p7.list1_2: **Contracts:** delivery offers and the contracts you hold.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p7.list1_5: **Crew:** hands looking for a berth; see [[pirates_n_ships:crew|Crew]].
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p7.text1: Every desk has a harbour master behind it, in a green frock coat and a peaked cap. Right-click him, or the {item:pirates_n_ships:harbor_desk}**harbour master's desk**, to open the port's market. If you strike him he waves you off for a while; if he dies, a new one takes the post after three days.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p7.text3: Stay within 8 blocks of the desk, or the market closes.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p8.heading: Prices
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p8.text1: Buying raises a price and selling lowers it, and prices drift back toward their usual level day by day. Buying and selling in one port always loses money; carrying a good from a port that makes it to a port that wants it pays, though less with every stack you sell.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p8.text2: The goods of the sea: sugar, fish, timber, iron, grain, hides, cocoa, gunpowder, {item:pirates_n_ships:tobacco}**tobacco**, {item:pirates_n_ships:spices}**spices**, {item:pirates_n_ships:cloth}**cloth** and rum. Spices fetch the most. Tropical ports grow sugar, cocoa, tobacco and spices; colder ports deal in fish, timber and iron; navy outposts sell powder.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p8.text3: Merchant convoys sail the lanes between the ports and move prices too: a port a convoy has just supplied pays a little less for what she brought.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p9.heading: Stolen goods
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p9.text1: Goods taken from a captured or sunk ship carry a plunder mark in their tooltip. Only a pirate fence buys them, at a heavy discount and with no questions. The desk's sell toggle chooses whether you sell clean or plundered stacks.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.p9.text2: A village or navy harbour master turns plunder away and reports you to the navy. And the navy looks into your hold: sail within sight of its soldiers or a fort with more than 16 marked goods aboard, under any flag, and you are suspected of piracy. Fence your plunder before you go near the navy.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.trade.title: Cargo and trade
pirates_n_ships.almanac.welcome.p1.text1: So you mean to go to sea. Good. Keep this book close, hand, for the sea forgives nothing twice and this Almanac holds what every captain before you learned the hard way: how to build a ship and sail her, how to keep a crew alive and willing, how to trade, how to fight, and how to keep clear of the hangman.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.welcome.p2.list1: Use it in your hand to read it wherever you stand.
Sneak and use it on a table or any surface to lay it down. A placed Almanac lies shut until someone opens it to read.
Turn the pages with the corner arrows, the arrow keys or the mouse wheel. Escape closes the book.
The ribbons on the edge are bookmarks, one per chapter. Hover one to read its name; click it to turn there.
Words in {#2e6a24}green ink{/} are tips worth remembering, and words in {#9a1c14}red ink{/} are warnings you ignore at your peril.
Names in {#2a4580}blue ink{/} lead to another chapter: click one to turn there.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.welcome.p2.text1: The {item:pirates_n_ships:captains_almanac}**Captain's Almanac** is bound from a book, two pieces of leather and two copper ingots.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.welcome.p2.text2: The book remembers where you left off and opens there next time.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.welcome.p3.text1: Some pages carry a **Show me** button. Press it and the Almanac shows you the thing being done, step by step, on a little model of a ship. Back out of the scene and you return to the same page.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.welcome.p3.text2: Hover over an item that has a scene, such as the cannon, and hold the Ponder key to watch it from your inventory.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.welcome.p4.headi: How this book is laid out
pirates_n_ships.almanac.welcome.p4.text1: Start with [[pirates_n_ships:first_ship|Your first ship]]: it takes you from a heap of planks to a ship under sail in a few pages. The chapters after it tell each part of the trade in full.
pirates_n_ships.almanac.welcome.p4.text2: The last pages are for the purser and the quartermaster: [[pirates_n_ships:inventory|The ship's inventory]] lists every block and item with a line on each, [[pirates_n_ships:ledger|The Quartermaster's ledger]] holds the settings and orders a server's keeper needs, and [[pirates_n_ships:not_yet|Not yet charted]] owns up to what is still missing.

The wind fills the cloth and it bellies out to leeward. Square sails like the wind from astern; within 30° of the wind no sail drives
Using an upper yard with an empty hand trims that one sail only

pirates_n_ships.ponder.shared.ship_assem: Blocks placed on her afterwards become part of her at once
Now she is one ship: she floats, rolls with the sea and keeps her hold dry
Build your ship from any blocks, right on the water: this hull keeps a dry hold below the waterline
To take her apart, sneak and use the helm with an empty hand and press Disassemble on the ship screen twice
Everything that touches the hull becomes part of the ship, so leave a gap of water to the shore or a dock
Place a helm on deck. Its helmsman stands behind it, and the way he looks is the bow
She must lie nearly still and level: her heading is rounded to the nearest quarter turn and her blocks are set back into the world
Air, water and terrain such as sand, dirt and stone are never taken along
Use the helm: every block connected to it, up to 2048, becomes one ship
pirates_n_ships.ponder.shared.ships_bell: In a navy outpost every bell rings the alarm when pirates come to raid it
Nothing else is tied to it: no watch, no order, and your crew does not ring it. It is your signal
Hang the ship's bell on a wall, or stand it in its frame on a post or any block with a firm middle
Three sticks over three gold ingots and an iron nugget make one
Use it to ring it: the bell swings away from you and rings out
Struck from the side, it rocks at half the swing
pirates_n_ships.ponder.shared.steering.c: Hard over she turns on a circle three to four ship lengths across, at any speed: slower only takes longer

pirates_n_ships.ponder.shared.swivel_gun: Hold use with an empty hand: it turns wherever you look, all round, from 30° down to 45° up

The swivel gun mounts on a fence, a wall, iron bars, brig bars or any block with a solid top
